data.title: Bond yields surge to fresh two decade highs as oil prices hit $105 per barrel
data.description: Key U.S. Treasury yields surged to fresh two-decade highs Thursday, as the price of oil returned to $105 per barrel. The yield on the 30-year U.S. Treasury bond soared as high as 5.446%, a level not seen in 22 years. After posting its biggest one-day rise since April 2025, the yield on the 10-year U.S. Treasury bond continued advancing on Thursday. In early trading it climbed as high as 5.15%. That remains its highest level since 2007. Meanwhile, oil prices jumped again overnight, after a mediated U.S. dialogue with Iran at the United Nations General Assembly produced no tangible evidence of any progress towards ending the 7-month war. Those rising oil prices have continued to push commercial diesel fuel prices to all-time records. On Thursday, the national average price for diesel was $4.51, effectively unchanged from a day earlier, but up 73% since the Iran war began. Likewise, the national average price of regular unleaded gas was 50% higher Thursday than it when the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in late February, at $4.48 per gallon. Stocks fell in early trading, putting them on track for a third straight day of losses. The S&P 500 was down by 0.5%, while the Nasdaq Composite declined 0.7%. The Dow tumbled almost 300 points. A global sell-off Around the world, the bond sell off is roiling sovereign debt markets. “The acceleration higher in US rates yesterday is being felt globally as to highlight for the umpteenth time that we’re all in this global bond boat together,” wrote Peter Boockvar, chief investment officer at OnePoint BFG Wealth. The yield on Japan’s 10-year bond rose to its highest level since 1996 on Thursday, while Germany’s 10-year bund notched its highest yield since 2009. “As summer officially ends, macro data are still fairly solid in the US, as indicated by a 4%-type unemployment rate and 2%-ish growth,” wrote Bank of America’s global rates analysts. “But the risks continue to pile up for anxious markets,” they added, pointing to ongoing trade wars, the energy supply shock, upcoming midterm elections and potential risks to the AI boom. One major driver of the surge in bond yields this week was a report from S&P Global, released Wednesday morning, which found that while U.S. business activity accelerated in September, “firms’ input costs have meanwhile jumped in September at the steepest rate for four years, with fuel and transport costs spiking higher.” That led investors and traders to ramp up their bets on Fed rate hikes. Federal Reserve Bank of New York President John Williams said the central bank still has more work to do to help bring down inflation. It’s “likely that another rate hike may be appropriate by the end of the year,” Williams said during a speech in London Thursday. Nonetheless, he said, the U.S. economy has demonstrated “remarkable resilience” in the face of “significant shocks” hitting it. Bessent’s next move The rise in bond yields has continued despite a series of measures taken — and warnings delivered — by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent earlier this month. “I am the house now” Bessent said on Sept. 8, “and you can bet against me if you want.” At the time, Bessent was defending a Treasury Department intervention to help prop up the Japanese yen. The hope was that a stronger yen would relieve pressure on the Japanese government to sell U.S. Treasury bonds. But it hasn’t entirely worked, and as of Thursday the Japanese yen had again weakened to levels on par with it’s exchange rate against the U.S. dollar from early September. Bessent has also intervened in the U.S. bond markets, buying back longer-dated Treasuries in an effort to keep their yields low. The next test for Bessent’s plan will arrive later on Thursday, when the Treasury Department is set to buy back up to $6 billion worth of 20- to 30-year bonds. In response to the department’s initial buyback earlier this month, bond yields rose — exactly the opposite reaction from what the administration intended. But Bessent has brushed off the stumble, insisting that the U.S. bond market is still the “best performing” in the world and crediting President Donald Trump for it. “If some of the Bloomberg Terminal bros are unhappy with what I’m doing, well, that’s too bad,” Bessent said in an interview Sept. 10. But not everyone is entirely convinced by Bessent’s swagger. “US Treasury Secretary ‘House’ Bessent seems to be demonstrating the house does not always win,” wrote Paul Donovan, chief economist at UBS Global Wealth Management, on Thursday morning.

data.title: Map: See how gas prices have changed in the county where you live
data.description: Gas prices are up across the country, but nowhere are they up as much as in Gregory County, S.D., where an average gallon of gas would run you $4.62 a gallon Thursday, 95% more than the price at the start of the Iran war. How much gas prices have increased depends on where you live, an NBC News analysis of average gas price data from AAA shows. Gregory County’s price was up $2.26 a gallon, while Kauai County, Hawaii, prices had only increased 91 cents as of Friday. It also depends on the state. In Indiana, average gas prices are up $1.14 per gallon, among the lowest state-level increases in the nation (Indiana has repeatedly suspended its state gas tax). But in Utah, the average price is up $2.18 per gallon, the largest state-level increase in the U.S. This map, showing the latest county-level gas prices and the change in prices since the start of the war, will be updated daily. Polling consistently indicates that prices and the economy rank among voters’ top issues ahead of the midterm elections. An April poll showed gas prices were a problem for nearly two-thirds of Americans. As of early May, counties have seen increases of an average of $1.47 per gallon. However, about 100 counties, mostly in Indiana and Ohio, have seen price increases of $2 per gallon or more. Conversely, a little more than a dozen counties — mostly in Georgia and Nebraska — have seen price increases of less than $1 per gallon. See the trends of gas prices nationally and on the state level with the NBC News gas price tracker, and calculate how much the gas price increase has cost you with the the NBC News gas cost calculator.

data.title: Toys ‘R’ Us is opening 120 new stores as grownup collectors fuel toy sales
data.description: Some people never seem to grow up. A resurgent Toys “R” Us is hoping to take that fact to the bank. The storied chain announced Thursday it was opening 120 standalone Toys “R” Us locations this holiday season. In total, 160 standalone stores will be open in time for Christmas, the company said. The chain is already featured at numerous Macy’s outlets across the country. Expect to see many adults and even teens shopping for themselves at these locations, in addition to the usual holiday shopping for kids. Toy sales among adult-only households have now outpaced households with children for toy sales, growing 16% through June, according to market research group Circana, equivalent to 55% of total toy industry receipts. Toy sales among all adults are growing 25%, only slightly behind the teen group at 33%. Together, teens and adults generated nearly 60% of the industry’s incremental dollar gains in the first half, Circana said. The trends have helped toys see their strongest overall first-half-of-the-year sales in six years. It’s part of a broader trend toward so-called “analog” products in an increasingly digital world. “We’re seeing toys increasingly function as hobbies, fandom ecosystems, and social experiences rather than traditional children’s products,” said Kristen McLean, vice president of client insights for Circana’s Entertainment Knowledge Group. “That’s expanding the consumer base and creating new opportunities for manufacturers and retailers that understand how to engage collectors, enthusiasts, gifters, and self-purchasers.” Toys “R” Us didn’t mention adult collectors in its announcement. The top toy brands today include Pokémon; major sports leagues like NFL, FIFA, and MLB; Marvel, Star Wars, Hot Wheels, and LEGO Botanicals, Circana said. Toys “R” Us named LEGO, Barbie, Hot Wheels, Pokémon, and KPop Demon Hunters as the top brands it plans to offer. In its heyday, Toys “R” Us had more than 1,000 locations across the United States. But it filed for bankruptcy in 2017 as it was boxed out by larger rivals such as Walmart and Amazon amid a broader downturn in brick-and-mortar sales as e-commerce began to boom. Today, Toys “R” Us is managed by WHP Global, a group backed by private equity that also oversees Babies “R” Us, as well as a suite of fashion brands including Express, Marc Jacobs and Vera Wang.

data.title: House passes bill to shield consumers from data center price hikes on energy
data.description: WASHINGTON — Under pressure to act on unpopular data centers, the House on Wednesday overwhelmingly passed bipartisan legislation aimed at shielding consumers from higher energy costs when new data centers are built in their communities. The vote was 417-3. Because GOP leaders brought the bill to the floor under a fast-tracking procedure known as suspension, support from two-thirds of voting lawmakers was required. The bill, dubbed the Ratepayers Protection Act, is the only legislation related to artificial intelligence that was scheduled for a vote this week as Congress considers its response to dire warnings from some former AI employees about its dangers. With the House holding its final votes before the midterm elections on Wednesday evening, and the Senate only staying in Washington a few more weeks, not much more is expected to get done to address the AI issue until at least the post-election lame-duck session. The data center bill was co-sponsored by Reps. Gabe Evans, R-Colo., and Kathy Castor, D-Fla., both members of the Energy and Commerce Committee. It aims to put the onus and responsibility on tech and data center companies — rather than consumers — to pay for power upgrades required to operate new large data centers. Specifically, the legislation would create a federal standard for state utility regulators to consider when creating rules for large, high-power data centers to cover the costs of power generation, transmission lines and other infrastructure upgrades needed to power these facilities, according to Evans. Data centers provide the computing power and storage for artificial intelligence. The Evans-Castor bill, however, does not address any of the recent warnings from AI researchers: that the fast-moving technology could cause human extinction. And it’s unclear what the Senate will do with the bill, if anything. The upper chamber has its own set of data center bills, but it hasn’t moved any. “Hardworking families should not have to subsidize the energy demands of data centers,” Evans said in a statement after the vote. “America needs the infrastructure to lead the world in AI and outcompete Communist China, but we cannot have that growth at the expense of hardworking families, farmers, seniors, and small businesses.” Evans, in his first term, is one of the most vulnerable House Republicans of the cycle; Cook Political Report characterized his race against Democratic state Rep. Manny Rutinel in Colorado as a “toss-up.” Evans and other at-risk lawmakers had been pressing GOP leaders for a vote on data centers, which have emerged as a key campaign issue in the November midterm elections. Trump has fully supported the construction of new data centers, saying they are critical for U.S.-based AI companies to compete with China. But voters in swing districts and swing states have argued that data centers are springing up across America too fast, and they’ve begun mobilizing against their construction in many places. A recent NBC News Decision Desk poll powered by SurveyMonkey found that nearly 70% of respondents oppose the construction of AI data centers in their neighborhood; 45% said they were strongly opposed. The ratepayer bill was just one of a handful of energy-related bills the House took up in its final week in session before the Nov. 3 midterm elections. The votes come as oil remains above $100 a barrel and the high cost of living and inflation remain the top issues heading into Election Day. Many Democrats supported the measure, saying they didn’t view the bill as harmful, but they panned it as weak. “Our communities and the people in our districts are so outraged, and they are understandably very angry that Congress isn’t doing enough” on data centers, Rep. Veronica Escobar, D-Texas, who represents El Paso, told NBC News before the vote. “I’m going to vote yes, but it is truly the bare minimum. In fact, it’s kind of pathetic that all we’re going to do is make them pay their own energy costs.” “These data centers are going into communities like mine that don’t want them,” she added. “My community does not want data centers, loudly and clearly, and I agree with my community.” Michigan Rep. Debbie Dingell, who heads Democrats’ policy and communications arm, voted yes but said, “It’s not enough in any way, shape or form.” And former Progressive Caucus Chairwoman Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., said before the vote that she might support the bill but pointed to President Donald Trump’s comments a day earlier that the AI industry doesn’t need guardrails and that serious safety warnings about AI are a “hoax.” “This is the same party that has a president that says that the AI threat is a hoax, and so I am worried about just allowing this to be, ‘Oh, we’ve solved it,’” Jayapal said. The effort “is a direct contradiction to what their president is continuing to say in opposing any real regulation.”

data.title: How Kraft Heinz is keeping its legacy brands affordable to cost-conscious shoppers
data.description: Years of high inflation have strained household budgets across America, putting a spotlight on the rising costs of necessities like gas and groceries. They have also contributed to a shift in how consumers perceive value at the supermarket. New research from McKinsey finds that Americans are increasingly turning away from name brand foods to lower priced, private-label or store-brand products. For Kraft Heinz CEO Steve Cahillane, these changes in the marketplace demand a shift in strategy. “We can’t just rely on having a strong brand and saying that’s going to be enough,” Cahillane said in an interview on a tomato farm in Woodland California, part of NBC’s Business in America initiative. “Consumers have only so many dollars available for their food budget in a month’s time, and so you have to earn the right to be in that basket each and every day.” In recent years, store brands have shed their traditional associations with lower quality ingredients and temporarily “trading down.” Today, 85% of consumers believe private-label grocery products are just as good or better than those from name brands, McKinsey reports. Kraft Heinz sells over 200 brands, many of them household names like Heinz ketchup, Kraft Mac & Cheese, Oscar Mayer meats, Capri Sun drinks, Miracle Whip spread, Velveeta, Philadelphia cream cheese and Kool-Aid. But this is a challenging time to be in the name-brand food business. Last year, Kraft Heinz’s net sales in North America were down about 5% from 2024. When Cahillane took the helm as CEO in January, he was tasked with turning the business around. One part of that strategy, he said, is deploying promotional discounts more strategically. “We’re working with our retail partners to make sure that at the beginning of the month, when consumers are really doing their big shops, that we’re out there with good offers across the board,” said Cahillane. Consumers in general tend to have more spending power at the beginning of the month when government benefits such as SNAP are distributed, paychecks arrive, and monthly budgets reset. “Promotions can be an effective means by which to drive that initial purchase,” said Erin Lash, a senior director of consumer equity research at Morningstar. But promotions can also create a new challenge: Getting shoppers to come back once the deal is gone. “Promotions can be kind of a slippery slope,” said Mark Mayer, associate professor of Marketing at Indiana University and a former Kraft Foods brand manager. If customers “only buy your product when they can get it for a deal,” then the promotion defeats its purpose, he said. Unlike store brands, a company like Kraft Heinz needs a pricing strategy that both appeals to shoppers and also protects the brand’s status and reputation for quality. “In general, competing on price is not great for established brands,” said Alexander Chernev, professor of marketing at the Kellogg School at Northwestern University. Unless a company is specifically positioned from the outset as a discount brand, slashing prices can undermine a brand’s identity. This is especially true for legacy products like those in Kraft Heinz’s portfolio. It requires Kraft Heinz to pull off a difficult balancing act: Making its products more affordable without diminishing the value of its brands. Cahillane said that when it comes to pricing, Kraft Heinz is not lowering list prices across the board. Only where the economics make sense. “The biggest price drop, where we’re bringing prices down, is most certainly in our coffee business,” which is home to brands like Maxwell House and Gevalia. A drop in global coffee prices strengthens the economic case for price cuts. As of Wednesday, benchmark coffee futures were down 30% from a year ago. Kraft Heinz is also offering some of their products in smaller sizes. “This isn’t shrinkflation,” said Cahillane, “this is recognizing that if we’re selling a 32-ounce bottle of ketchup and that’s too much for a family… we have a smaller eight ounce bottle at a very affordable price.” It’s a strategy that has also been utilized by other major packaged food companies, including PepsiCo, Campbells, and Mondelez, as they look to offer shoppers lower-priced options. Ultimately, Kraft Heinz must give shoppers a reason to pay full price, said Cahillane. And quality is what will justify the premium. “Value is affordability, but it’s also delivering the product quality and the promise that you’re making to consumers,” he said. “If they buy your brand, they’ll be receiving a value that they’re willing to pay for.”

data.title: Tracking U.S., state and county gas prices, in maps and charts
data.description: The war in Iran has led to higher prices at the gas pump. Gas prices in the United States, up by more than 40% since the U.S. and Israel launched the war, have soared as the global oil supply constricts. Now at a national average of more than $4 per gallon, according to data from motor club AAA, this price increase is straining already-stretched budgets in households across the country. NBC News is tracking gas prices and how they change at the national, state and county levels, and will be updating this article daily with the latest data. Average gas prices have increased more than a dollar since the U.S. and Israel first attacked Iran. In six states — Alaska, California, Hawaii, Oregon, Nevada and Washington — average gas prices are at more than $5 per gallon. Indiana, Mississippi and Texas are paying the least, according to AAA data. According to a Brown University analysis, the increase in gas prices since the start of the war has cost Americans more than $50 billion. Fuel costs aren’t limited to gas. Jet fuel prices have been surging as well, leading airlines to increase airfares. Oil prices have spiked, then see-sawed, were approaching pre-war levels, and are now surging again as turmoil in the Middle East continues. Since mid-May, the average national gas price has decline by around 30 cents. The average price is still up more than a dollar per gallon since the start of the war.
